en: The Purification of the Commentary titled *Vajrapradīpa*, a Sādhana of Śrī Hevajra.
Oṃ, homage to Śrī Hevajra!
Having first prostrated to Śrī Hevajra, whose nature is free from waves [of conceptual thought], [I shall compose this work].
Relying upon the stage of generation (utpattikrama), the purification will be explained clearly.

First, the Sūtra of the Means of Achievement (*sādhanasūtra*) is proclaimed: Now, the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*), the four divine abodes (*caturbrahmavihāra*), the supreme innate (*parama-sahaja*), one’s own chosen deity (*sveṣṭadeva*), the protection-circle (*rakṣācakra*), the resolve on emptiness (*śūnyatādhimokṣa*), the charnel grounds (*śmaśāna*), the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), the causal maṇḍala (*hetumaṇḍala*), the swift descent (*drutāpatti*), the arising (*samutthāna*), the placement (*nyāsa*), the nature of hatred (*dveṣātmā*), the emission (*utsarga*), the wisdom-circle (*jñānacakra*), the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), the sealing (*mudraṇa*), the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), the activity for the world (*jagatkārya*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), the rising (*utthāna*), mantra recitation (*mantrajāpa*), the reality of the offering (*balitatva*), the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*), the second placement (*dvitīyanyāsa*), the wandering (*viharaṇa*), eating (*bhojana*), conduct (*caraṇa*), sleeping (*śayana*), and rising again (*punarutthāna*). By this, the thirty-two features of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) are purified. At the outset, the yogi is one whose mind is intent upon the welfare of sentient beings. A "yogi" is one whose character (*śīla*) is to desire yoga.

"Sattva" refers to one whose mind is intent on the welfare of beings because he desires to fulfill their aspirations. "Having properly propitiated the venerable Guru according to the ritual procedure" means having been established in the supreme maṇḍala of Śrī Heruka. By this, it is meant that having become completely settled and abandoning physical pride, one should propitiate the venerable Guru with a perfectly focused mind. "Propitiation" means knowing the tradition of the Guru’s correct instructions. When there is such propitiation of the venerable Guru, one is initiated into the maṇḍala spoken of by Heruka according to the ritual procedure. "Initiated into the maṇḍala spoken of by Heruka" means being consecrated according to the proper sequence—from the water initiation up to the initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*). "Initiated according to the proper sequence" means being correctly authorized; having been consecrated, once the disciple is known to be fit and a worthy vessel according to the traditional instructions, one should then reveal to him the Tantra and the ultimate reality, beginning with the *viramānanda* [joy]. Other matters should be taught by way of examples such as dreams, illusions, and mirages. "Correctly authorized" means that the practitioner, so authorized, should practice the sequence to be described in secret until he attains the *mudrā*. "Attainment of the *mudrā*" means some degree of attainment. This is called "having attained the knowledge of the extremely pure and non-erroneous reality."

It is "non-perverted" (*aviparīta*) because it does not become otherwise. However, having abandoned the impurity of this ordinary body, one knows through the gateway of the perfectly pure knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). They say that knowledge has attained the path by means of knowledge; thus, by this, one has attained the perfectly pure and non-perverted knowledge of reality. Now, regarding the phrase "one who has obtained the sign" (*labdhanimitta*): the "sign" (*nimitta*) is the conceptualized form. When there is the attainment of the perfectly pure and non-perverted knowledge of reality, the pillar (*stambha*) is the cause of non-perverted knowledge, and the non-perverted knowledge of reality is the effect. One knows that sign according to tradition; by this, it is the sign of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇanimitta*). Therefore—
Fire is known by smoke, and water by the crane;
the lineage of the wise Bodhisattva is known by these signs.

By the word "and" (*ca*), it is further indicated that a yogi endowed with wisdom, desiring to accomplish the glorious Hevajra, should go to a cremation ground or a forest once he has obtained a lotus-lady (*vidyā*) as described in the root text. Thereafter, staying in a delightful place and having performed offerings of *bali* and worship, he should, through secret yoga and according to the prescribed ritual, bring forth the wheel of worship (*pūjācakra*) and offer sprinkling, water for the feet, water for sipping, the *argha* offering, immersion, and the waving of lamps (*nīrājana*). Having fully worshipped with the specific outer, secret, and essential (*tattva*) offerings, he should begin the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Then follows worship with various kinds of flowers and so forth, and instrumental music with lutes and other instruments.
The secret of the meditation on the substances of the ritual pledge (*samaya*) held in the hands, situated within the circle of goddesses located in that wheel.

The reality known as the *saṃhāradravyavigraha* (the form of the substance of withdrawal) vibrates together with *Nairātmyā*. He who worships in this manner—that Lord of the Mandala (*cakrabhaṭṭāraka*) brought forth by the network of rays from the seed-syllable situated in the sun of the friend—is present before him; by this, the meaning of "emerging from the seed-syllable situated in the sun of the friend" is indicated. Then, one should perform the sevenfold unsurpassed worship before him. By this, the wheel of worship has been described by the Blessed One for the sake of the accumulation of merit. For, "From the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of gnosis comes supreme enlightenment. Thus ends the section on the wheel of worship. 1.

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is characterized by the love one has for an only son; having generated this toward all sentient beings and constantly perceiving them all as fallen into the ocean of *saṃsāra*, and seeing that just as it is painful when a son suffers in prison, so too is it for these refuge-less beings, the yogi generates great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Thereafter, having attained great joy (*mahāprāmodya*), the practitioner, considering himself as one who has achieved success, should cultivate sympathetic joy (*muditā*) while filled with such delight. One should cultivate great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), which is characterized by total detachment from attachment to *saṃsāra*, the acquisition of greatness, honor, and the like. Thus are the four divine abodes (*caturbrahmavihāra*). ||2||
The mantra practitioner who has become thus should begin the supreme sādhana:
first, the wise one should meditate on the corpse as being of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*;
the yogin, standing upon it, should visualize himself as Heruka.

Having established oneself there as Śrī Herukavajra, one should bring face-to-face the meaning of the six syllables. Through the authentic instruction beginning with “The syllable *Śrī* is non-dual gnosis,” and so forth, one should meditate up to the face by means of the yoga of the samādhi of Jñānālokavajra, which is the meaning of the four syllables of *Śrī Heruka*. “Supreme, with the luster of a moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*)”—thus [ends] the supreme. (3)

Having discarded this impure body by means of this [method], one should begin the practice of Sahaja-yoga. It is stated that instantly, in the center of the Buddha-abode, by means of the syllable *Evaṃ*, one should meditate upon oneself as Vajrasattva—greatly peaceful, with matted locks in a crown, two arms, one face, and three eyes; seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, holding the Dharmamudrā with both hands, standing upon a moon disc atop a corpse on a *viśvapadma*; pervading infinite world-realms, possessing the thirty-two major marks and adorned with the eighty minor signs; one should contemplate Sahaja-Heruka as being of the nature of the three beings (*trisattva*). Thus ends the section on Sahaja. (4)

Therefore—the union of *āli* and *kāli* is the supreme state of selflessness; this is the meaning of the corpse, the seat of Vajrasattva. His generation through the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* is not intended. Why? Because of the word "syllable" (*akṣara*), which means "empty. Therefore, if the mass (*piṇḍa*) arises from the non-conceptual, it is for that very reason the cause for the stabilization of this mass arising from the syllable. And it was said by the Blessed One in the eighth chapter: "The union of *āli* and *kāli* is the seat of Vajrasattva;
for the mass arising from the syllable, the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are not intended."

As before, [one should meditate on the deity] with its faces, marks, and so forth, according to the statement, "having the luster of a moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*). Having visualized Sahaja-nātha by means of the word *sattva*, one should begin the stage of Dveṣavajra. Next, I shall explain the stage of Dveṣavajra through the application of the syllable *jraṃ*: having visualized a sun by means of the letter *ra* in the heart, one should contemplate a full moon by means of its bindu. Within that, by means of the letter *ja*, one should visualize the syllable *hūṃ*, which indicates the seed of the birth of the world. Thus, having visualized the Lord of the Three Worlds—that is, within his heart, meaning within the heart of Vajrasattva—how? According to the sequence described in the Chapter on Deities.
One should visualize the syllable *raṃ* within one’s own heart, which becomes a solar mandala;
and right there, one should visualize the syllable *hūṃ*, whose nature is wisdom and means.
One should visualize the syllable HŪṂ, which is black in color, most terrible, born from the vajra,
situated in the center of the vajra-navel, and is the reality of HŪṂ.

One should visualize the vajra, produced from the syllable *Dīṃ* and distinguished by the [prefix] *vajra-*, together with the agent; this is how it should be understood. Then, having seen [the seed-syllable] transformed from the syllable *Hūṃ*, one should manifest oneself as the essence of Hatred (*dveṣa*). By means of the sound "transformed from the syllable *Hūṃ*," having transformed all of this—the moon and so forth—one should manifest the Vajra of Hatred in the heart according to the oral instruction.

Oṃ Vajradhṛk Hūṃ Bhagavatī. Aṃ: one should emit [the seed-syllable] into the space of the sky; one becomes the essence of Vajra-dveṣa (Vajra-hatred). One should meditate on the form established by the sequence to be described: a body equal to that [of the deity]. In the midst of the four [deities], the yogi should cultivate [the central deity] according to his resolve (*adhimokṣa*). According to the oral instruction, he should visualize the threefold form consisting of the three beings (*trisattva*), having the appearance of his own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), with eight faces and so forth, most terrible—such is the Lord he should cultivate. This is because of the statement: "One should cultivate the Lord of the Maṇḍala, arisen from the reflection of the being (*sattva*)."
In this way, one should emanate [the deity] through the yoga of Hatred-Vajra, by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart; thus is one's chosen deity. (5)

One should emit the assembly of wrathful deities (*krodhasaṃghāta*) in the cardinal and intermediate directions in their proper order—all transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ* and filled with great masses of blazing rays. Thus, one should meditate on Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, and Vighnāntaka in the cardinal directions starting from the east, respectively. They are black, white, red, and blue; they hold a vajra-mallet, a white vajra-staff, a red vajra-lotus, and a terrifying vajra; they are dwarfish and pot-bellied; and their heads are marked by Vairocana, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya. Then, in the intermediate directions starting from the northeast, one should meditate on Acala, Ṭakkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, and Mahābala. They are intensely black and hold a sword, a hook, a staff, and a trident. Acala and Ṭakkirāja are graceful, adorned with divine ornaments, and have distorted faces. One should meditate on Nīladaṇḍa and Mahābala as having faces distorted like those of Yama and Vaṭuka in the center of that [group]. Furthermore, above is Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, yellow in color, holding a yellow wheel; he wears a crown of Vairocana and is dwarfish and pot-bellied. Below is Śumbharāja, black in color, holding a club.
Kharva, Lambodara, Ṭakkī, and the others—these four [have] Śumbharāja as their lord, who wears a crown of Akṣobhya. These [are they].

The ten wrathful deities (*krodha*) should be visualized standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, holding a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and a noose (*pāśa*) in their left hands, upon sun discs on universal lotuses (*viśvābja*). Having thus sequentially emanated the wrathful ones, one should contemplate that they have gone to their respective places; then, because they are standing facing [the practitioner], one should join the palms in the *saṃpuṭāñjali* gesture and, preceded by praise with the eight-line heart-mantra and sub-heart-mantra, look at them as they ask, "What shall we do? Then, according to the distinctions of pacifying rites (*śāntika*) and so forth, one should command them with the mantra beginning "Oṃ śumbha niśumbha... for the wise one. Having received the command from Vajradhara, they establish their own emanations in their respective places; then, going themselves, they bind the hosts of obstructors (*vighna*) by the throat with a vajra-noose, terrify them with their respective weapons, seize them, and returning, they hand over the obstructing beings to their respective emanations in the ten directions and stand facing Vajradhara—thus one should visualize. In this regard, the host of obstructors is as follows: Indra is fair-complexioned, thousand-eyed, wearing a jewel crown, and of graceful form. Yama is black, with upright reddish-brown hair, short and pot-bellied. Varuṇa is white, his head marked by hoods, and of graceful limbs. Kubera is yellow, wearing a jewel crown, and of graceful form. Īśāna is white, wearing a crown of matted locks (*jaṭāmukuṭa*), short, and large-bellied. Agni is red, his head marked by a crown of matted locks, and of short body. The Rākṣasa is smoke-colored, with loose hair and a short body. Vāta is dark-blue.

[The deities are as follows: Ratnamukuṭī has a graceful body. Above is Pitāmaha (Brahmā), yellow in color, with a skull-cup (*kharva*) and a protruding belly (*laṃbodara*), wearing a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmukuṭī*). Below is Pṛthvī, yellow, wearing a jewel crown, with a dark-blue and graceful body. These Vighnas and Vināyakas, seized by Yamāntaka and the others, should be visualized as terrified, agitated, and intent on seeking protection. Thereafter, from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, one should emanate below a black-colored, most terrible *śūla* (spear) that is unbearable like the fire of universal destruction (*pralaya-anala*), and above, [emanate] the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī. Having offered these to Yamāntaka and the others, one should contemplate them upon the heads of the hosts of obstructors (*vighna-gaṇa*). Thereafter, one should drive in the stakes (*kīla*) with this mantra: *Oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ phaṭ kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ vajrakīla vajradhara ājñāpayati sarvaduṣṭavighnānāṃ kāyavākcittavajraṃ kīlaya kīlaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ.* This is the mantra for the staking. With this mantra: *Oṃ vajramudgara vajrakīlaya ākoṭaya ākoṭaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, the wrathful deities strike. All [the deities], having visualized themselves as a vajra-hammer through the transformation of their own emblems, strike the stakes with the mantra until they reach the surface of the earth.

They would have departed. Then, one should visualize Yamāntaka and the others having entered their respective emanations. Thereafter, at the time of unification, one should see the retinue of Vināyakas utterly destroyed by the fire of the wrathful deities.
Now—having visualized the sun in front by means of the syllable *repha*, [one should place] a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) born from *hūṃ* upon that navel.
With that very same vajra, one should visualize a surrounding wall and a cage-like enclosure.

By means of the syllable *ca*, one should visualize [the protection wheel] extending as far as the depths of the netherworld (*mārasātala*), established by a net of vajra-arrows, a canopy of vajras, and a ground composed of vajras; for it is said, "one should expel the obstructors" (*vighnānutsārayet*). This wheel of protection is for the purpose of pacifying obstacles. (6)

Thereafter, one should recite the mantra that encapsulates the essence of the reality of all phenomena without exception. In truth, through the investigation of all dharmas, whatever form arises—that is the essence; one should cause its encapsulation, that is, its gathering, to enter the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) of the entire world. One should dissolve the protection wheel into the light-ray of the seed-syllable in the heart; the light-ray into the Vajra of Hatred (*dveṣavajra*); the Vajra of Hatred into the Knowledge Commitment (*jñānasamaya*); the Knowledge Commitment into the Samādhi Commitment (*samādhisamaya*); and finally, the *hūṃ* should be withdrawn in due order. Then, reciting the mantra: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra of the Wisdom of Emptiness," one should immediately realize the meaning of the mantra and, through the conviction in emptiness (*śūnyatādhimokṣa*), perceive the three realms as being without appearance. (7)

One should meditate on Wisdom (Prajñā), who pervades the space-element in their midst, arising from the syllable *HŪṂ* as the Source of Phenomena (Dharmodayā), empowered by the seed-syllable, uniform in form, and white. "Above that" means above the space in their midst; there, the earth arises in sequence with the colors of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas], consisting of twelve spokes. Through this dissolution of the mandalas of the four great elements in the fixed order beginning with wind, one should contemplate the celestial palace adorned with the eight cremation grounds upon a pedestal of a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*).

Now the cremation grounds are described according to their sequential order: In the east is the great cremation ground named Caṇḍogra. There is the elephant-faced [deity] of great supernatural power, white, seated upon a Śirīṣa tree. Indra is the lord of the direction; he is fair-complexioned, thousand-eyed, and seated upon the white Airāvata. Vāsuki is the king of serpents, yellow; Garjita is the cloud, of universal color; Sumeru is the mountain, composed of the four jewels; and the shrine named Śvetavajra is white. (1)

To the south is the great cremation ground named Karaṅkabhīṣaṇa. Beneath an *āmra* tree is the guardian of the direction Yama, black in color, possessing great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), with the face of a buffalo and mounted upon a buffalo.

The serpent (nāga) is Padma, white in color. The cloud is Āvartaka, of variegated colors. The mountain is Malaya, pale yellow (*gaura*). And the shrine (*caitya*) is named Piśunavajra, black in color. ||2||

In the west is the great cremation ground named Jvālākula. At the Aśoka tree is the white, highly powerful Makarānana. Varuṇa, the lord of the quarter, is white; the nāga Karkoṭaka is red; the terrible cloud is of variegated color; Mount Kailāśa is white;
and the caitya named Saṃjñāvajra is white. ||3||

In the north is the great cremation ground named Gahvara. At the Aśvattha tree is a being with a human face, possessing great supernatural power (maharddhika), who is fair-complexioned. Kubera is the guardian of the quarter; he is fair-complexioned and has a man as his vehicle. Takṣaka is the nāga; he is black. The swirling cloud is of all colors. Mount Mandara is dark blue.
The shrine (caitya) named Cittavajra is fair-complexioned. ||4||

In the northeast is the great cremation ground named Lakṣmīvana. At the banyan tree is Gomukha, white and of great supernatural power. Maheśvara is the guardian of the direction, white, with a bull as his vehicle. The nāga Śaṅkhapāla is yellow. The cloud Caṇḍa is of variegated colors. Mount Mahendra is black. The shrine named Vāgvajra is white. (5)

In the southeast is the great cremation ground named Aṭṭahāsa. On a Karañjaka tree is Chāgānana, who is red and possesses great supernatural power (maharddhika). The guardian of the direction, Hutāśana, is red and has a goat as his seat.
The nāga Mahāpadma is dark green. Ghana is a cloud of variegated color. Mount Gandhamādana is yellow.
The shrine named Kāyavajra is red. ||6||

In the southwest is the great charnel ground named Ghorāndhakāra (Terrible Darkness). There is a corpse-faced being of great supernatural power on a *latāparkaṭī* tree; he is black. The directional lord is the Rākṣasa, seated upon a corpse, who is black. The nāga is Ananta, who is white. The cloud is Pūraṇa, of variegated colors. The mountain is Hema, which is white. The shrine is named Ratnavajra, and it is black. (7)

In the northwest is the great cremation ground named Kilikilārava. On the Pārthiva tree dwells the one named Mṛgānana, who possesses great supernatural power and is dark green in color. The guardian of the northwest direction is Māruta, who is dark green and mounted upon a deer. The nāga is Kulika, who is variegated in color. The rain-cloud is Viśvavarṇa, and Śrīparvata is blue.
The caitya is named Dharmavajra and is dark green. ||8||

And in their midst are those of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*); furthermore, on the left, the hell-guardians (*naraka-pāla*) are to be visualized as agitated, with their hands filling their mouths with blood; on the right, they are to be visualized as possessing lotus-hands in the gesture of grasping various flavors. Following that, [the charnel grounds] are dense with various trees composed of green meadows, fresh sprouts, and leaves; they are graced by flocks of various birds such as crows, cuckoos, owls, parrots, mynas, pigeons, female pigeons, vultures, and so forth; they are filled with various beasts such as lions, wolves, tigers, bears, boars, and the like; they are crowded with flowers of various fragrant scents; they are filled with swarms of various serpents; and in various places, they are strewn with skeletons, skulls, bones, corpses, fat, and so on.

They were adorned. Furthermore, in various places, they were filled with hosts of male and female meditators (*dhyāyin* and *dhyāyinī*), male and female adepts (*yogin* and *yoginī*), male and female *avadhūta*s, male and female *yakṣa*s, male and female *preta*s, male and female *rākṣasa*s, male and female *kumbhāṇḍa*s, male and female *bhūta*s, male and female *ḍāka*s, and male and female *vīra*s, who dwell in monasteries and meditation-houses, by ponds, and in groves. Some were intent on thoughts fixed upon the conventions of the *samaya*. Others were filled with groups of *ḍāka*s and *ḍākinī*s engaged in laughter, dance, embracing, kissing, and various other [pleasures]. Following that, some danced with vajra-steps with minds full of bliss, while others sang with vajra-songs.

Some were practicing various vows and conducts; some were consuming the five nectars and the five lamps; some were offering various articles; some were gratifying various sentient beings; and some were to be seen drinking intoxicants. Others were playing various musical instruments, such as the *ḍāka*, *ḍamaru*, *paṭaha*, *mardala*, *kṛpīṭa*, *jharjhara*, lute, flute, pipe, and cymbals. Furthermore, they were completely filled with hosts of gods, asuras, garuḍas, and their male and female counterparts—such as the *siddhas*, *vidyādharas* and *vidyādharīs*, *mahoragas* and *mahoragīs*, *kinnaras* and *kinnarīs*, and *gandharvas* and *gandharvīs*. Resounding with shouts of joy, those terrifying and formidable abysses were utterly heart-gladdening through the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the nine dramatic sentiments (*navanāṭyarasa*), and remained presided over by throngs of *vetālas* and spirits. Eight—

One should contemplate the cremation grounds. The eight cremation grounds are the purification of the eightfold consciousness; the "eightfold consciousness" refers to the five consciousnesses beginning with the visual consciousness, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the afflicted mental consciousness (*kliṣṭamanovijñāna*). These are illustrated by the examples of a mirror, a dream, an illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, an echo, the moon in water, and space. Therefore, through the thorough knowledge of all phenomena, the eight cremation grounds are devoid of subject and object. Thus, the cremation grounds are known by way of these analogies for the eightfold consciousness. (8)

Now, the peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra) transformed from the four great elements—wind and the others—is described. Through the purification of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), it has four gates; through the four right efforts (prahāṇa), it has four archways (toraṇa).

[They] are remembered [as follows]: through the purification of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the four altars (*vedikā*) are formed; the five faculties (*indriya*) and the square vajra-line are the five faculties and the square vajra-line; the five powers (*bala*) are the four corners, the *hāra* (necklace), and the *arddhahāra* (half-necklace); and through the purification of the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), the eight pillars are fashioned. The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are the eaves, the gables, the parasol, the fly-whisk, the canopy, the bell, and the banner. One should meditate on the gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*) as radiant, purified by the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). By the word "gabled chamber," [it is meant that] its essential nature is the meaning of the factors conducive to enlightenment; however, regarding its origination, it should be understood as stated above. In its own form, one should meditate on the sequence of earth and so forth. Now, the divisions of the factors conducive to enlightenment are explained. By the grace of the venerable Saroruhapāda: first, there is the origination of the body therein. From that phenomenon (*dharma*), all phenomena are empty.
Therefore, the body was produced first.

By the word *anu*, its state—which is the nature of that phenomenon—is indicated; subsequently, because there is an absence of the arising of mindfulness of that phenomenal nature, the "prior form," which is the intrinsic nature of the reality of all things, is called by the word *smṛti* (mindfulness), as it is the nature of the mind. If one asks how it appears through that imagined aspect, [the answer is] that it does not exist otherwise than in its own nature. Furthermore, it appears exactly like a reflection in a mirror. Regarding its arising, what is meant by the word *upasthāna* (establishment) in relation to the imagined aspect? It is called *upasthāna* because it stands (*sthāna*) in the highest (*uttama*) of the high; it is the supreme, luminous state referred to by the word *smṛti*. For the sake of abiding in that establishment, one should conceive of the eastern gate as being thus. Through the purification of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*), there is the eastern gate. Likewise, through the purification of the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna*), there is the southern gate. Likewise, through the purification of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*), there is the western gate. Likewise, through the purification of the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittānusmṛtyupasthāna*), there is the northern gate. If it is so, how can feeling exist apart from form?

And elsewhere it is said that even perception (*saṃjñā*) and the formative factors (*saṃskāra*) are likewise [unreal]. However, just as an illusion, a dream, or a city of the Gandharvas, so do the gates appear. Thus, all phenomena (*dharma*), including form, sensation, perception, and formative factors, are manifested by consciousness (*vijñāna*); and since even consciousness itself is unreal and cannot withstand analysis, how can these phenomena manifested by consciousness be momentary entities? This is the statement of the Śākyas. Therefore, consciousness too is momentary. How so? Because all phenomena—such as pots fashioned from gold and other materials—are analyzed away. Just as there is no substance in the absence of those properties, so in the absence of all phenomena, there is no consciousness. For this very reason, consciousness is also momentary. Just as there is no subject (*grāhaka*) in the absence of an object (*grāhya*), and just as there is no grasping (*grahaṇa*) in the absence of both subject and object; furthermore, just as the subject exists depending upon the object, so the act of grasping exists depending upon both subject and object. In the absence of those two, there is no grasping. Indeed, the remaining form—the Great Gate—is not known without the purity of its arising. Thus, the fourfold gate of the elements is to be meditated upon. The nature of the light of emanation (*nirmāṇāloka*) consists of the four foundations of mindfulness, which are remembered as the four archways (*toraṇa*).

It is the antidote for unarisen evils; the severance of arisen evils; the production of unarisen roots of virtue; and the dedication of arisen roots of virtue toward awakening—namely, the antidote, the severance, and the production-dedication. Of what is it the antidote? It is the antidote to the afflictions such as passion (*rāga*). Since the affliction will arise from that [passion], this antidote constitutes an opposition to its arising. Furthermore, even when passion and other afflictions have already arisen, their severance occurs through this cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for the sake of their destruction.

Therefore, from the destruction of this [obscuration], there is an absence of worldly attachment (*āmiṣa*). Precisely for this reason, the arising of the state free from affliction (*nirāmayapada*) occurs; this is "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*), which is the desire to act in common with all sentient beings. Through the purity of the four abandonments (*prahāṇa*), there are the four archways (*toraṇa*). Through the purity of the four bases of miraculous power (*ṛddhipāda*), there is the fourfold altar (*vedikā*). These are: zeal (*chanda*), energy (*vīrya*), investigation (*mīmāṃsā*), and mind (*citta*). Zeal (*chanda*) is the state of absolute non-attachment toward what is to be contemplated. Likewise, energy (*vīrya*) is the state of absolute longing, which is uninterrupted continuity. By that very [energy], "investigation" (*mīmāṃsā*) is the constant examination. Furthermore, "examination" (*vicāra*) is the making of that [object] one's own form through both self and other, by means of that very [energy]. "Mind" (*citta*) refers to the production of the aspect of its own nature, culminating in the mind. Therefore, the culmination of the mind is direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). Thus, the four bases of miraculous power are purified. The fourfold altar is the production of miraculous power (*ṛddhi*). That which is the aspect of the purity of emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is called its "expanding and contracting form," according to one's wish.

Supernatural power (*ṛddhi*): it is the production of the direct realization of this form. Therefore, without this, there is no entry into the palace of the *vajra* of one’s own nature. The five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*) constitute the square and the *vajra*-lines. These are: the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). The first cause of firm conviction is designated by the term "faculty of faith. The second is "activation" (*pravartana*); through extreme devotion, it proceeds with self-knowledge, and having abandoned the non-cessation of consciousness, it proceeds toward the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) for those engaged in the activities of *saṃsāra*. This is designated by the term "faculty of energy. It is yoga day and night in reality. The third is "mindfulness" (*smṛti*); when the self-consciousness is severed, that which is the uncontrived arising of whatever form occurs merely by the entry of the mind is called mindfulness. This is designated by the term "faculty of mindfulness. The fourth is "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*); here, the word "supreme" (*agra*) refers to the correct path. Being of one essence with that is "one-pointedness of mind," which is termed the "essence of concentration" (*samādhisattva*). This is designated by the term "faculty of concentration. Thus, by these four faculties, the [mandala] is square. By the word "chest" (*urasā*), it is not meant anything else. Regarding the "vajra-lines": the five lines and the five walls are differentiated according to the divisions of the five Tathāgatas. In their center is the Buddha-palace; by the word "vajra," it is equal to everything. The "vajra" is indivisible and is designated by the term "faculty of wisdom" (*prajñendriya*). It is the non-abiding of all phenomena (*sarvadharmāpratiṣṭhāna*).

If it has been established [that they are equal], then the walls are equal; thus, there is no mutual distinction among the Tathāgatas by virtue of their nature as Vajradharas. One should contemplate the meditation chamber as adorned with these walls, which are decorated with vajra-threads. The four corners are adorned with necklaces (*hāra*) and half-necklaces (*arddhahāra*). Regarding the "five powers" (*pañcabalāni*): they are the power of faith (*śraddhā*), the power of vigor (*vīrya*), the power of mindfulness (*smṛti*), the power of concentration (*samādhi*), and the power of wisdom (*prajñā*). Faith is the first cause; it is the conviction (*abhisaṃpratyaya*). The fulfillment of that cause is its power, its capacity, and its realization. Because it brings this about, it is designated by the term "power of faith. Vigor is so called because, having made the mind firm and uninterrupted, one sets it in motion. Mindfulness is so called because consciousness is not perceived there even for a moment, since one is engaged day and night. Concentration is the one-pointedness of mind directed toward things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*). By the word "as they truly are," the non-apprehension of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-anupalambha*) is meant—the supreme path. Because it realizes that, being non-different from it, that realization is designated by the term "power of concentration. Thus, the four corners are purified by the four powers. Because they bring about the fulfillment of the four faculties (*caturindriyāṇām*), they are the four powers. By the word "fulfillment," the fulfillment of the goal is intended. By the power of wisdom, the necklace and half-necklace are realized; the previously mentioned power is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). That which is the non-abiding in all phenomena—that is the complete realization. Because it is non-different from that, the meditation on the necklace and half-necklace by means of the power of wisdom is thus described. There are eight [corners] by means of the Noble Eightfold Path.

The pillars are thus conceived: the non-abandonment of what has been undertaken is Right View (*samyagdṛṣṭi*); speech that is non-deceptive is Right Resolve (*samyaksaṃkalpa*); not transgressing the ten wholesome paths is Right Speech (*samyagvāk*); thinking without harming sentient beings is Right Action (*samyakkarmānta*); a mind focused solely on the ten wholesome paths is Right Livelihood (*samyagājīva*); the ultimate realization of selflessness is Right Effort (*samyagvyāyāma*)—effort being the severance of existence and non-existence; knowing the three times as a single moment is Right Mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*); and the single form of the three worlds is Right Concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). By these, the pillars are conceived. The seven limbs are known as the bird, the step, the head, the parasol, the fly-whisk, the canopy, the bell, and the banner. Constantly remembering and knowing the three times is the limb of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*). Unceasingly awakening great beings is the limb of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasambodhyaṅga*). Proceeding by means of uninterrupted great yoga is the limb of enlightenment of the investigation of energy (*vīryapravicayasambodhyaṅga*). Having no delight other than selflessness is the limb of enlightenment of the investigation of joy (*prītipravicayasambodhyaṅga*). Constantly practicing the yoga inseparable from emptiness and compassion is the limb of enlightenment of the investigation of tranquility (*prasrabdhipravicayasambodhyaṅga*). Attaining the unerring reality is the limb of enlightenment of the investigation of concentration (*samādhipravicayasambodhyaṅga*). Proceeding effortlessly within concentration is the limb of enlightenment of the investigation of equanimity (*upekṣāpravicayasambodhyaṅga*). By these limbs of enlightenment, the bird and the others are said to be meditated upon. By this, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—

Through the differentiation of the dharmas of the wings [of awakening] and culminating in the meditation on the peaked pavilion, the complete awakening to omniscience regarding emptiness and so forth is first described. Thus ends the section on the peaked pavilion. 9.

Now, the generation of the Causal Vajradhara is described. Within the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), upon the pericarp of a multi-petalled lotus, the four Māras should be visualized as being trampled by the sun. By means of the *He*-vajra, [the four Māras are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and Devendra. These four Māras—Body, Death, Affliction, and the Son of a God—are the creators of affliction for the aggregates (*skandhas*). Then, having seen [a moon disc] trampled by the sun above that, one should visualize a moon mandala arising from the transformation of those [syllables], having doubled them by means of the vowels beginning with *A* in both direct and reverse order. This indicates the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and has the nature of the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Having added the six syllables *Ka*, *Ḍa*, *Ḍha*, *Da*, *Dha*, *Ya*, and *La* from among the consonants beginning with *Ka*, and having doubled them by viewing them in both direct and reverse order, one should see a sun mandala arising from that transformation. This indicates the eighty minor marks and has the nature of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*). In the center of these two, having seen the two seed-syllables *Hūṃ* and *Aṃ*, one should see a skull-cup and a flaying knife marked with a double vajra (*viśvavajra*) produced from them. Marked by the two seed-syllables, this has the nature of the Discerning Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). Emitting rays of light from the seed-syllables, which illuminate infinite world-systems, and causing them to re-enter [the seed-syllables], one should contemplate all of them as one; this is the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). All of this transforming instantaneously, one becomes the form of Śrī Heruka, which is the Wisdom of the Perfectly Pure Realm of Phenomena (*suviśuddha-dharmadhātu-jñāna*). By this, the five aspects [of wisdom] are to be understood. The form as it was seen by the Mirror-like Wisdom is made of one taste (*samarasī-kṛta*) by the Wisdom of Equality.

That which has been examined by the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is likewise made into a single unity by the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). Thus, the wisdom of the utterly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*) is of one form together with all aspects; this is the awakening through five aspects (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*). Having thus perceived the single form of the three worlds, one should then visualize, in order, Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Rudra at the eastern and other gates, and likewise Vaivasvata, Vittanāyaka, Nairṛti, and Vaimacitriṇa in the corners starting from the northeast (*aiśānī*). Having thus visualized these eight seats, one should see the eight seed-syllables—*gaṃ*, *caṃ*, *vaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *puṃ*, *śaṃ*, *caṃ*, *ḍaṃ*—in the midst of the union of moon and sun upon them. One should contemplate the emblems of Gaurī and the others, transformed from those [seeds]: a knife, a sword, a tortoise, a snake, a lion, a mendicant’s bowl, a wheel, and a vajra. Having unified everything into one, presided over by each of those [emblems], Gaurī and the others are to be produced and visualized. Khacarī, Bhūcarī, and Nairātmā are to be seen in the lotuses of body, speech, and mind according to the root mantra. By this, the mandala to be meditated upon has been described. Their colors, emblems, and so forth will be explained later. As for their purification: now, "compassion" (*kṛpā*) refers to the redness of the eyes; "compassion" is the affection consisting of a single-mindedness toward sentient beings, and by that, the eyes are red. "Black-bodied" (*kṛṣṇāṅga*) is due to the mind of loving-kindness (*maitracitta*); "mind of loving-kindness" means the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-faculties (*indriya*). By that mind of loving-kindness, the purification of the black body and eyes is achieved. Through the "three vajras," there is the warding off of body, speech, and mind; the "three vajras" are remembered as the four feet (or bases) by means of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), namely: generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency of purpose. Inconceivable...

The attribution of the mind to reality is the bestowing of names. Regarding that attribution of the mind to what is mindless, one should understand that joy arises as it pleases, according to the instruction. Just as gold [is tested] by burning, cutting, and rubbing on a touchstone, so too is reality described by the term "pleasant speech. Furthermore, conduct that accords with the body, speech, and mind is described by the term "beneficial conduct" (*artha-caryā*). By the term "common purpose" (*samānārtha*), this very state of having a single form with all is meant; this is the purification of the four conducts. The eight blisses are purified by the liberations (*vimokṣa*); such is the form.

One perceives emptiness; one perceives emptiness as having no space; one perceives emptiness entered into the knowledge of the auspicious and inauspicious; one perceives emptiness created by wrong views; one perceives emptiness entered into space; one perceives emptiness entered into nothingness; one perceives emptiness entered into the knowledge of selflessness; one perceives emptiness. One perceives emptiness as the cessation of consciousness. Thus, there are eight doors purified by liberation. "Liberation" refers to having entered the bliss liberated from all dualities. By means of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), there is the cessation of the knowledge of the consciousness of self and other. The sixteen arms are the pure sixteen emptinesses—the sixteen emptinesses being: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, [and so forth].

The sixteen emptinesses are: great emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, emptiness without beginning or end, essential emptiness, non-essential emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

Now the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is explained: the emptiness of the end of all phenomena is "internal emptiness" (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*). All external phenomena are likewise "external emptiness" (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). That which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion, according to the appropriate instruction of the Guru, is "internal-external emptiness" (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). Due to the yoga of non-differentiation, that which is experienced is designated as "great emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*). That which is empty because of the great yoga, and which is empty of emptiness, is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). For this very reason, since the ultimate (*paramārtha*) is more excellent than the most excellent, it is the "emptiness of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). These are the six emptinesses. When these are conditioned and unified in every aspect, it is "conditioned emptiness" (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). There is no unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nor even non-conditioning (*asaṃskāra*); being endowed with the unity of all aspects within the birth [of reality], it is "unconditioned emptiness" (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). It is endowed with the excellence of all aspects.

There is no distinction between that and absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), nor with beginningless and endless emptiness (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*). "Intrinsic emptiness" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) means that intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) arises in five aspects; since these five aspects are empty of aspect, intrinsic emptiness is the absence of self-nature (*svabhāva*); thus, the intrinsic nature of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the emptiness of extreme intrinsic nature (*atiprakṛti-śūnyatā*). All phenomena—whether stationary or moving, even down to a single atom—are expressed by the term "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*); that which is so expressed is all empty, and this is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). Regarding "non-existence" (*abhāva*): what is this world? It is like a firebrand-circle (*alātacakram*); the perception of existence is empty of its own form, its intrinsic nature, and its designated self-nature—this is the emptiness of the non-existent nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Regarding "self-nature" (*svabhāva*): "self" (*sva*) refers to the excellent mind (*sucitta*); since even the mind is non-existent, this is the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Just as form (*rūpa*) would arise from the unification of the space element and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), so too has the emptiness of the nature of non-existence been declared. These are proclaimed as the pure arms of those [deities]. Now, the purity of the facial colors is described: the first face is black for the sake of accomplishing the activity of hatred and for restraining the senses; the left face is red for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*). This is the unification of body, speech, and mind.

By virtue of their intrinsic nature: the right [hand] is white for the sake of pacification. Within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the pure deities have the nature of the syllable *haṃ*; they are peaceful, with faces turned upward, and smoke-colored (*dhūmra*), possessing a terrifying appearance.

In the west, for the sake of destroying arisen afflictions (*kleśa*), there are hatred and the rest, as well as arisen affliction itself. For the sake of destroying the four Māras, there are four faces resembling bees. The Māra who is the basis of the aggregates (*skandha*) is the *skandhamāra*; the death-Māra (*mṛtyumāra*) is the nature of death belonging to the aggregates. The affliction-Māra (*kleśamāra*) is likewise that which causes harm to sentient beings. The Devaputra-Māra is said to be the craving for women. Thus, for the sake of destroying the fourfold Māra, there are four faces resembling bees. The purification of the symbols (*cihna*) is now described: elephants and the others are taken up for the pacification of various afflictions. "Various afflictions" means:
Cough, asthma, insanity, consumption, leprosy, and scabies;
as well as splenic disorders, tuberculosis, and diseases characterized by the forms of elephants and so forth—these are proclaimed [as the afflictions].

Thus are the eight afflictions (*kleśa*). The meaning is that these sentient beings, who have become like elephants, are supported upon the vessel-world (*bhājana*). To signify the attainment of the eight sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*) over the elements such as earth and so forth, the symbols held in the left hand are:

"Sovereignty over the body, sovereignty over speech, sovereignty over the mind, as well as supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), omnipresence, sovereignty, and the power to act according to one's will—these are the eight qualities. Thus it is said.

Mastery over the body (*kāyaiśvarya*) is [the power] to manifest bodies without end; mastery over speech (*vagaiśvarya*) is [the power] to speak in all languages; mastery over mind (*cittaiśvarya*) is [the power] to know the minds of sentient beings; mastery over supernatural powers (*ṛddhyaiśvarya*) is [the power] to see various world-systems through supernormal faculties; omnipresence as the single form of the three worlds is mastery over omnipresence (*sarvagataiśvarya*); mastery over desire (*kāmaiśvarya*) is [the power] to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings through great bliss by means of desire—provided that "desire" is understood here by the word "will" (*icchā*); mastery over agency (*kartaiśvarya*) is the state of being the agent, the Holder of the Vajra (*vajradharatā*); and mastery over qualities (*guṇaiśvarya*) is the movement in the form of the deity from within profound nirvāṇa, and the wandering in the form of the deity from within nirvāṇa. By this, the purification of the [deity's] marks (*cihna*) is explained. Now the purification of the vessels (*bhājana*) is described: the vessel is the manifestation of the limb of compassion (*karuṇā*). The arms are purified by emptiness (*śūnyatā*); by this, the inseparability of emptiness and compassion is established. The five fingers are the five Buddhas; "finger" (*mātra*) refers to the consort (*mudrā*).

The five Tathāgatas are pure. Regarding the "seal" (*mudrā*), it refers to the [six] ornaments: the wheel, the earring, the necklace, the bracelet on the wrist, the armlet, and the girdle; together with the ashes, these are proclaimed as the six seals.

The "six mudrās" refers to perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Perfect knowledge is that wherein there is an absence of [ordinary] cognition; that which is the true nature within the absence of cognition is perfect knowledge. The garland of heads (*śiromālikā*) fashioned from the fifty letters is upon the shoulders; it is the *āli*, the purification of the fifty letters. The garland of heads upon the neck reveals the path of the unified state (*yuganaddha*), and it is also described as the nine dramatic sentiments (*navanāṭyarasa*).

Now, [one should visualize] oneself as the Blessed One endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments (*nāṭyarasa*): the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) which is of one flavor with selflessness (*nairātmya*); the heroic (*vīra*) through dwelling in the charnel ground; the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) with a face made formidable by a frown; the furious (*raudra*) with blazing radiance; the comic (*hāsya*) with a wide-open mouth; the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) adorned with a garland of moist heads; the compassionate (*karuṇā*) with a mind intent on favoring sentient beings; the marvelous (*adbhuta*) in its illusory form; and the peaceful (*śānta*) because of having abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as passion and the rest. The Blessed One is joined with these nine dramatic sentiments. As the causal basis, he wears a garland of five dry heads upon his forehead, which demonstrates the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of the five aggregates (*skandha*). His head is marked with a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all beings. He has three eyes due to the thorough knowledge of the three bodies (*kāyatraya*). In each of his faces, he possesses the form of the Omniscient One. His tawny hair stands upright to demonstrate the burning away of all afflictions such as passion. All—

Nakedness is for the purpose of demonstrating that phenomena are free from obscuration (*dharmanirāvaraṇa*). The half-lotus posture dance (*ardhaparyaṅkatāṇḍava*) is performed because he has attained the state of awakening (*bodhipada*). The display of only a single big toe is for the purpose of demonstrating that the entire triple world is his single form. The Blessed One (*Bhagavān*) is also a false appearance; as is the Blessed One, so too is the Blessed Lady (*Bhagavatī*). Furthermore, regarding their distinction: by virtue of being the single form of all, she has one face, and her hands are busy holding a skull-cup filled with the blood of the Vāma-devas and Asuras. What is meant by the term "deva-asura"? "Deva" refers to body, speech, and mind, while "asura" refers to their objects. The emptying out of these two is the filling of the skull-cup. This unification of the skull-cup and the blood demonstrates the fulfillment of the meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). In her right hand, she holds a flaying knife (*kartṛ*) for the purpose of cutting through all afflictions (*kleśa*). Whatever else remains should be understood as being similar to the purity of the Blessed One, and likewise for the Blessed Lady.

Now, one should meditate upon the four wheels within the body of the Vajradhara who is the object of attainment (*sādhya*). Having performed whatever emanations and so forth are required, for the sake of benefiting [beings] according to their needs through reality (*tattva*), the four wheels—purified as the four bodies (*kāya*) of Dharma, Enjoyment, Emanation, and Great Bliss—should be meditated upon. Now, the purification of the mandala deities (*māṇḍaleya*) is explained: Gaurī and Kṛṣṇā are for the purpose of awakening those beings who are to be disciplined by Māra.

In the right [hand], she holds a knife to cut through wrong views; in the left, a Rohita fish to destroy the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of cyclic existence. She is Gaurī, red in color, for the sake of awakening those beings who are to be trained through passion (*rāga*). In the right, she holds a *kṛpīṭa* (a type of vessel) to demonstrate the nature of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*); in the left, a boar for the purpose of destroying delusion (*moha*). Vetālī has the luster of molten gold, for the sake of training those beings who are to be nurtured—that is, for the purpose of generating bliss. In the right, she holds a tortoise to demonstrate emptiness (*śūnyatā*); in the left, a lotus vessel which is the essence of compassion (*karuṇā*). Ghasmarī resembles an emerald, with a slightly reddish-green hue like a stone. She is for the accomplishment of rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*) and for awakening those who are nihilistic. In the right, a snake due to the purification of hatred (*dveṣa*); in the left, a yogic bowl (*yogapātrikā*) consisting of wisdom and means. Pukkasī is blue, for the purpose of paralyzing in ritual practice and for awakening those beings who are conceited (*mānin*). In the right, a lion to tear asunder the armies of Māra; in the left, a dagger (*puṣku*) to sever all dualities. Śavarī is white, for the purpose of awakening peaceful beings. In the right, a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) to demonstrate the five wisdoms; in the left, a *khiṅkhirikā* (a small vessel) to awaken the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñāna*).

Caṇḍālī, dark blue as the sky, is for the accomplishment of the purpose of paralyzing and for awakening those whose minds are stagnant; in her right hand, the discus for the sake of cutting away even slight knowledge, and in her left, the plough for the purpose of uprooting the impurity of ignorance. Ḍombinī, variegated in color, is for the accomplishment of the purpose of obstacles and for awakening those of cruel disposition; in her right hand, the vajra for the demonstration of indivisible gnosis, and in her left, the threatening gesture for the intimidation of all the wicked. The purification of the eight seats of these goddesses is now described.

Now, eight seats have been shown for the purpose of cutting off the eight types of extreme attachment—namely, attachment to passion (*rāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), hearing (*śravaṇa*), drinking (*pāna*), eating (*bhojana*), sleep (*nidrā*), reasoning (*tarka*), and purity (*śuddhi*). Furthermore, one must maintain extreme detachment during meditation. Thus, the purification of the eight seats has been described. All these [deities] are to be visualized and meditated upon as having three eyes, with tawny hair standing upright, adorned with the five mudrās, standing in a dancing *ardhaparyaṅka* posture, naked, with faces made terrifying by fangs, and endowed with the desire for the Blessed One. Immediately after this, on the row of deities, starting from the right of the main entrance, there are two goddesses at each of the junctions of the door corners, beginning with the primary [deity] named Vīṇā, and so forth.

This is the seed-syllable of Āsā, conjoined with the perishable lunar drop (*indubindu*) and marked by the sign of its generated meaning. Furthermore, one should contemplate that just as Gaurī and the others arise when the [mandalas] between the moon and sun are seen, so too is there the production of Vīṇā and the rest. Now, Vīṇā is yellow, Vaṃśā is red, Mṛdaṅgā is smoky-grey, Murujā is white, Mālā is yellow, Lāsyā is red, Gītā is dawn-red, Nṛtyā is multicolored, Puṣpā is white, Dhūpā is black, Dīpā is golden-hued, Gandhā is yellow, Ādarśā is white, Rasā is red, Sparśā is green, and Dharmā is white. These hold their respective symbols in their hands; they are in dance postures and seated upon moon-discs. They are to be visualized as purified by the sixteen vowels. This is the realization of the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatā-abhisambodhi*), beginning from the universal lotus and so forth, up to the completion of the image of the Holder of the Causal Vajra within the maṇḍala of deities. Thus ends the Causal Maṇḍala. (10)

Now, one should meditate on the subtle nature of the maṇḍala as red, encircled by two rows of *hoḥ* syllables. Having drawn in the gandharva-being, who consists of great bliss and is characterized by intense passion, by means of one’s own light rays according to the oral instruction, and upon his mere entry, the Blessed One—having become of a single flavor with the absolute supreme great bliss—melts through the passion of great desire together with his consort (svavidyā) and comes to abide in the form of a seed-syllable. Thus is the melting (*drutāpatti*). ||11||

Then the four goddesses, Pukkasī and the others, considering themselves protectorless (*anātha*), fell into great despondency. Being exceedingly longing and seeking to awaken his mind, they rouse him with these verses. Herein, the meaning of this tetrad of awakening verses is explained, beginning with: "Arise, O Lord, whose mind is the essence of compassion," and so forth. "Arise, O Blessed One, whose mind is always compassionate! Protect me, Pukkasī, through the yoga of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). Indeed, abandon desire for me; [arise] from the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and its fluid nature. I am yours through Great Loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*); without you, I am dead. Arise, O Hevajra, whose own nature is emptiness! May the body of Śavarī be perfected. I am yours through Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). "Having invited the worlds, O Lord of Passion, abide in emptiness! Why do I, the Caṇḍālī, address you? Without you, I burn; I see no direction, nor do I perceive any quarter. Therefore, arise! I am yours through Great Joy (*mahāmuditā*). "O Magician, arise! I know your mind. Even though you remain having performed a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), we Ḍombīs are exceedingly refined and cut through all mental constructions. Do not create a separation from compassion! I am yours through dwelling in Great Equanimity (*mahopekṣā*). Thus, by means of the purification of the four realities (*catustattva-viśuddhi*).

The swift-footedness (*drutā-patti*) has been demonstrated. These are the reality of the self (*ātma-tattva*), the reality of the deity (*devatā-tattva*), the reality of the mantra (*mantra-tattva*), and the reality of gnosis (*jñāna-tattva*). Here, it should be understood according to the sequence [of the] instructions from the Guru. The meaning of these four realities has not been explained here for fear of excessive prolixity. Therefore, if the Blessed One were to arise in person through the application of the song of reality (*tattva-gīta*), he would do so like one awakened from a dream; yet such a consequence is impossible. If the Blessed One were to become non-self (*nairātmyaka*) through a single-minded state together with absolute selflessness (*atyanta-nairātmya*), then [he would vanish], and thus [the practice would be] in the sky.

What does he see in a dream? Or rather, how does the Blessed One abide like one awakened from a dream? To this it is said: sentient beings do not know anything at all during the state of sleep; yet, how is their arising observed? It is by the power of their intention (*bhāva*) that they should arise suddenly, as if terrified. Likewise, the Blessed One, having entered the meditative absorption of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), does not perceive the consciousness of self or others; nevertheless, impelled by the song of reality (*tattva-gīta*), he arises through the force of his vow (*praṇidhāna*). Thus there are two questions: [how do] living beings [arise], and [how do they] not [arise] while clinging to physical pleasure?

"Do they know? [This refers to] the state of sleep; however, while the body exists, how could there be such an arousal on the part of the Blessed One? Furthermore, first the impure body was purified by the minister through the purity of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because of the attainment of attachment to the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Again, whose melting does this belong to? It does not belong to the emanation body—how so? Because it is devoid of bone and marrow. These are two questions. To this he says: "First, the melting occurs due to the cause, not the fruit. Moreover, this is the explanation of the means for grasping the essential nature, just as [it occurs] through the purity of emptiness and so forth. The grasping of the Causal Vajradhara is likewise through the purity of the melted state and so forth; the grasping of the Resultant Vajradhara is also the fruit. Thus, one question is refuted. Likewise, the other: first, there is the absence of an impure body in the form of the deity. In the absence of an impure body, there is merely attachment to the pure emanation body. Due to the absence of that [attachment], he remains in the form of consciousness (*vijñāna*) which is like a dream or an illusion, like liquid nectar or the moon. Therefore, he is the support for the aspiration of illusory consciousness. Just as an illusion does not know the perception of self or other, yet performs its function, so too the illusory consciousness, without the knowledge of self or other, for a long time...

One arises by the force of the momentum of one’s previous vow (*praṇidhāna*). The sequence for this arising is as follows, through the application of five aspects: "From the liquid nectar comes the form of the moon. Through the transformation of that liquid nectar, there is the *bodhicitta* consisting of the five gnoses (*pañcajñāna*). Among these, the moon is the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*) transformed from the syllable *A*; the sun is the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*) transformed from the syllable *Ka*. The seed-syllable and the emblem situated between them are called the discerning gnosis (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*). The single performance of all [these] is the accomplishment of the image (*bimba*), which is the pure reality (*śuddhadharmatā*). Then, by means of the rays arising from the *bodhicitta* composed of the five gnoses, one brings the entire world of moving and non-moving beings and the deities of the maṇḍala into a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) right there; thus, one should behold the *bodhicitta* in the form of the autumnal moon-disk—this is the meditative absorption of yoga (*yogasamādhi*).

Thereafter, one should meditate upon that which has instantaneously transformed into Sahaja Hevajra, who has the form of the autumnal moon, illuminates infinite world-realms, is joined with Dharmamudrā, and consists of the five gnoses; this is the samādhi called Anuyoga. ||12||

Then one should begin the placement (*nyāsa*) of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases: one should place the syllable *aṃ* upon form; the syllable *oṃ* is prescribed for feeling; one should contemplate *hrīṃ* in long perception (*saṃjñā*).

One should place *uṃ* upon the formative factors (*saṃskāra*). Upon consciousness (*vijñāna*), however, one should place the syllable *tvaaṃ*, through the purification of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). One should place the syllable *oṃ* upon the flesh; furthermore, one should project *ṛṃ* upon the blood. One should place *ṝṃ* upon the seminal essence (*bodhicitta*), and *lṛṃ* upon the marrow and fat, through the purification of the elements (*dhātu*). One should place *lṝ* upon the object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), and *eṃ* upon sound (*śabda*). One should place *aiṃ* upon the portion of odor (*gandha*), and *oṃ* again upon taste (*rasa*). One should place *auṃ* upon touch (*sparśa*), and *aṃ* upon the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). This is for the purpose of making these firm. And it was said by the Blessed One in the ninth chapter:
Vajrā is in formative predisposition (saṃskāra), Gaurī is traditionally taught to be in sensation (vedanā),
Vāriyoginī is in perception (saṃjñā), and Vajraḍākinī is in mental formations (saṃskāra).
The Yoginī Nairātmyā abides as the aggregate of consciousness in form;
Gaurī is proclaimed to be in form, and Caurī is celebrated in sound.
Vetālī is in the portion of smell, and Ghasmarī is remembered in taste.
Bhūcarī is renowned in the sense of touch, and Khecarī arises from the dharmadhātu.
Pukkasi is known by means of flesh; Śavarī is proclaimed to be in blood;
Caṇḍālī is said to be in semen; and Ḍombī is in fat and marrow.
Thus is the placement [of the deities], including the Vajradhātvīśvarī embraced by the Sahajanātha. This is the meditative absorption (samādhi) called Atiyoga. ||13||
By this, the arrangement of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases [is explained]. And likewise, from that [text] again:
"First is the awakening to emptiness; second is the gathering of the seed-syllable;
third is the perfection of the image; fourth is the placement of the syllables."
At the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, there is a quartet of lotuses;
at the wheel of emanation (nirmāṇacakra), there is a red syllable *a* facing upward, possessing five rays of light.

On the petals of the eastern and other directions of the *dharmacakra*, which is white and blue, is the syllable *hūṃ*: *vuṃ*, *aṃ*, *jrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, *hūṃ*. On the intermediate petals likewise, the *saṃbhogacakra* is red and faces upward; it consists of the syllable *oṃ*, which is red and encircled by the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*). The *mahāsukhacakra* is white and faces downward, consisting of the syllable *hūṃ*. [These are] four—

Having meditated upon the sixth, eighth, sixteenth, and thirty-second [fingers] in their respective order, one should contemplate the world of moving and non-moving beings therein. Then, according to the sequence stated in the *Mantrapatala* and following the traditional oral instructions, one should perform the empowerment of the three bodies (*kāyatrayādhiṣṭhāna*): by means of the syllable *Oṃ*, the Vajra-body; by means of the syllable *Āḥ*, the Vajra-speech; and by means of the syllable *Hūṃ*, the Vajra-mind. This is the Mahāyoga.

Now, "above that" means in the heart of the sentient being; according to the previously mentioned sequence and also the sequence stated in the *Sādhana*, one should likewise [visualize] the form of Śrī Heruka—either as the Solitary Hero (*ekavīra*) in the center of the four or as one's own chosen deity Nairātmyā.

One should visualize oneself as having entered [meditative absorption], endowed with one's own vidyā, or as the perfected form [of the deity]. Immediately following this, one should commence the threefold commitment (*samaya*): the commitment of the pledge (*samaya-samaya*), the commitment of gnosis (*jñāna-samaya*), and the commitment of meditative absorption (*samādhi-samaya*). Among these, Vajradhara is the commitment of the self; the sun at the heart is the commitment of gnosis; and the syllable *HŪṂ* above that is the commitment of meditative absorption. The two commitments of gnosis and meditative absorption are to be understood from the instructions to be explained hereafter. Furthermore, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the Blessed Lady just as for the Blessed Lord. Moreover, the superior practice concerns the Blessed Lady, wherein there is a collection of the five families (*pañcakula-kalāpa*). In the practice of the higher and lower, the term "collection" (*kalāpa*) is well-known as the assembly of Tathāgatas. One should visualize a three-petaled lotus produced by the syllable *ĀḤ*, a lotus filament by the syllable *HŪṂ*, a five-pronged vajra born from the syllable *HŪṂ*, and the *OṂ* at its jewel-center. Having empowered [the body] with the two verses beginning with "OṂ, the support of lotus-bliss," etc., one should move the vajra preceded by the recitation of the unstruck syllable (*anāhatākṣara*) and begin the rapture (*rati*).

In the midst of the five Tathāgatas, from the syllable *haṃ* as Vāgvajrā, there is the samādhi called Ādiyoga, beginning with the meditative absorption on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and ending with the bliss of delight (*ratisukha*). (14)

And this [wisdom] has emerged from the bodhicitta that arises as the great bliss of the unity of wisdom and means. Having understood this, one should practice within the city of the Mother (mātṛpura) preceded by the utterance of the three principles (*tritattva*), using the vajra-tongue. Reciting: "Oṃ! All phenomena have the nature of the vajra-worship of all Tathāgatas; Oṃ! I am of the nature of the vajra-worship of all Tathāgatas," the yogin, bearing the Garuḍa-mudrā, should thus perform the worship of the Tathāgatas constantly, even externally. Whether the wisdom-consort (*prajñā*) is auspicious or not auspicious, one must not fail to do so with her, for it would constitute a root downfall (*mūlāpatti*). Having worshipped all the Tathāgatas in the place of one's own body and resolved, "I satisfy them," thereafter, whatever exists—even a mere atom, a fragment, or a drop of the essence of bodhicitta—by its transformation, one should visualize the goddess in the center of the lotus, together with the maṇḍala and its deities, and the Lord. Through the yoga of churning and being churned: Oṃ Vajradhṛk! Bhagavatī Āṃ! Gaurī Gaṃ! Caurī Caṃ! Vetālī Vaṃ! Ghasmarī Ghaṃ! Pukkasī Puṃ! Śabarī Śaṃ! Caṇḍālī Caṃ! Ḍombinī Ḍaṃ!

Immediately thereafter, by means of the passage beginning with "one should also perform the emission (utsarga) of Gaurī and the others," [the deities] are placed in the eastern and other doors in due order; these are the eight goddesses, Gaurī and the rest. Having emitted the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady, the Blessed Lord enters by means of two *hūṃ* syllables, and likewise the Blessed Lady enters the Blessed Lady. From the entry of the Gandharva-sattva up to the emission of the maṇḍala, this constitutes the awakening to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). 15.

Thereafter, one should meditate upon Gaurī and the others, who have arisen from the emission of the *bodhicitta* and are seated upon lunar discs. Furthermore, Bhūcarī, Khecarī, and Nairātmyā should be visualized as having entered for the sake of the Lord’s emission, entering in sequence into the previously mentioned locations. Thus, having correctly contemplated the mass of light rays—contained within the mandala circle as described, surrounded by the host of Vidyās, and pervading the expanse of the sky.

Now, one should perform the attraction, entry, binding, and pleasing of the wisdom-circle (*jñānacakra*). Emanating rays of light from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart, one should expand them throughout the expanse of space, summon the wisdom-circle, and visualize it before oneself. Having offered the water for honor (*argha*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, and having worshipped and praised it, one should perform the attraction, entry, binding, and pleasing with the mantra: *oṃ vajragauri ākarṣaya jaḥ*, and so on, using *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*. Having caused the wisdom-circle to enter the commitment-circle (*samayacakra*), they become unified as they please; one should maintain the divine pride (*devatāhaṃkāra*) [of being the deity]. This is the contemplation of the wisdom-pride within the heart. Although the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) is like oneself and the sentient beings, nevertheless, immediately after the entry, one should contemplate the wisdom-being in one’s own heart as red, two-armed, single-faced, and joined with Prajñā. Within that heart, one should likewise contemplate the Lord of Samādhi, and then the Blessed Lady and the others, such as Gaurī and the rest. Through the sequence beginning with the attraction of the wisdom-circle up to the entry of the wisdom-being into the wisdom-circle, there is the "complete awakening in all aspects" (*sarvākārābhisambodhi*). (16)

Thereafter, at the time of unifying the *jñānacakra* and the *samayacakra*, one should visualize that by means of blazing rays of light, the five Tathāgatas—having assumed the form of Heruka and consisting of the maṇḍala—are drawn from the expanse of space. One should then behold [the deity] praying: "May all the Tathāgatas confer empowerment upon me! Then, those Tathāgatas, with hands joined holding the five victory vases, themselves perform the bathing while reciting the verse beginning: "Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth," and so forth. One should visualize [this] with the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśriye hūṃ*. Thereafter, a rain of saffron, sandalwood, various fragrant perfumes, and flowers falls; the sound of drums resounds, and a tumultuous clamor from infinite world-systems arises through the sounds of dance, music, and praise. This is the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). (17)

Once consecrated on the head, he becomes Citteśa. One should then seal the Blessed Lady, who has Citta as her consort, along with Citteśa, Śāśvata, Ratneśa, and Amitābha, by means of Gaurī and the other goddesses. Furthermore, one should mark Pukkasī and the others on the heads of these Buddhas in their respective order. Then, Vīṇā and the others worship the Lord with their respective objects: the mirror, the lute, the perfume, the conch, the vessel filled with various flavors, the object of touch, and the Dharmodaya filled with the *bodhicitta*. Taking these, Rūpavajrā and the others worship the Blessed One.

"O Yoginī, you attend upon me for my well-being; O you who have obtained the boon within your own heart, may you awaken that very [nature] which is the compassionate heart of the entire world of moving and unmoving beings. Alas!
This is a deceptive act of rashness; O Heruka-Vajra, enough with this deluding glory! Thus it is said.

Through the vajra song, Locanā and the others praise the Blessed One. The Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Vidyādevis, Krodhas, and so forth, standing face-to-face in the sky, praise him with the heart-mantras, near-heart-mantras, garland-mantras, and eight-line mantras. One should then empower [the deity] with: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas*. By this—beginning from the empowerment and ending with the praise—the consecration at the crown of the head (*mūrdhābhiṣeka*) is completed. (18)

Thereafter, one visualizes before oneself a wind mandala arising from *yaṃ*, marked with banners; above that, a fire mandala arising from *raṃ*, marked with flames; and above that, a lotus vessel arising from the syllable *āḥ* placed upon three skulls, which is further empowered by the syllable *āḥ*. In its center is the red [liquid], white on the outside, and within it are the syllables *buṃ āṃ jrīṃ khaṃ hūṃ lāṃ pāṃ tāṃ vāṃ*. Having transformed these, one produces the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*). Above that, one sees it covered by the syllable *oṃ*, with a moon disc arising from *āḥ* and empowered by the syllable *hūṃ*. Through the heat of the fire fanned by the wind, it becomes like a single drop of mercury. One performs the purification with the syllable *hūṃ*, the awakening with the syllable *āḥ*, and the kindling with the syllable *oṃ*. Thereafter, having brought the wisdom-nectar (*jñānāmṛta*) through rays of light from the three principles (*tritattva*), one causes it to enter into that very place.

With the mantra *oṃ āḥ sarvatathāgatajñānāmṛte hūṃ*, one should touch the offering vessel with the vajra-hand. Having unified [the contents], stirred them with the *bhava-vajra* by means of *hūṃ*, and rendered them of equal flavor (*samarasīkṛta*), one should visualize the vajra dissolving into the nectar. Through the entry of the nectar of the Tathāgatas’ wisdom, it becomes exceedingly cool. Having thus accomplished this and empowered it with the three principles (*tritattva*), one should draw [the nectar] in with the tongue born of the *bhava-vajra* by means of light rays and consume that wheel as oneself. Reciting: *oṃ sarvatathāgatāmṛtāsvādavajrātmakāḥ sarvadharmāḥ; oṃ sarvatathāgatāmṛtāsvādavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, one becomes filled with bliss. From the initial tasting of the nectar until its conclusion, there is a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) following the successive stages. Thus ends the tasting of the nectar. (19)

Thereafter, by means of the yoga of its radiance, he goes to wherever there are disciples to be trained—having emanated himself in whatever form is appropriate for each—and having trained them, he returns and dissolves [the emanations] into his own respective bodies. Having proceeded in this very sequence, he should begin the cultivation of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-bhāvanā*). This is the meditative absorption named *Maṇḍalarājāgrī*, beginning from the emission [of light] up to the fulfillment of the world's welfare. (20)

Then, having seen the seed-syllable of the Great Mantra King, the Universal Monarch (cakravartin), in the center of the union of the sun and moon, one should meditate on the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Why? Because from the mass of light rays emanating from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated within the sun and moon at one’s own heart, one should first meditate on the Lord of Samādhi in the heart of the Jñānasattva.
