Having transformed that [syllable] into black and visualized it in the form of a drop (*bindu*), one should subsequently emit the syllable. One should understand this emission of the syllable in two ways by means of the term "emission" (*visarjana*) after having meditated on the subtle yoga to be described: the "syllable" (*varṇa*) refers to the Tathāgatas, such as the syllable *HAṂ*, according to the distinctions of the peaceful rites and so forth; the word "emission" (*visarjana*) refers to the explanation of the means of entering the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*). Then, having expanded and withdrawn [the syllables] from the inhalation and exhalation of the *ālikāli* [vowels and consonants], one enters therein oneself and becomes one. Having expanded the row of *ālikāli*, from where? From the inhalation and exhalation. By the path of inhalation, the *ālikāli* are emitted through the path of exhalation. Having emerged, one purifies the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) with those light rays, and having become one with the moving and non-moving world, one enters therein. Having withdrawn Gaurī and the others, as well as Nairātmā, oneself should abide in the state of Vajradhara through conceptualization and all phenomena. Therefore, [he is] two-armed, one-faced, and white. Where?
"Within the union of the sun and moon" means the yoga of the non-perception of existence and non-existence.

For this very reason, it is remembered as "enjoyment" (*saṃbhoga*) for the sake of attaining the unerring reality. It is the supreme Śiva, the reflection of sentient beings, free from the utterances *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
And so, in the *Kulapaṭala*, it is called "enjoyment":
Great wisdom, though residing within the body, is free from all conceptual constructions;
it pervades all things, and although situated in the body, it is not born of the body.
And so,
just as a form endowed with all its limbs appears most clearly in the reflection of a mirror,
even so is the body of Vajradhara, always possessed of the eighty minor marks and the [major] characteristics.
This is the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*); from the benefit of the world up to the innate (*sahaja*), it is the awakening in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*). ||21||

What is the meaning of "it remains in the state of the seed" (*bījāvasthā*)? That seed is the innate (*sahaja*). In this context, it should be remembered that laughter, gazing, embracing, and union are to be understood through the fourfold purification (*caturviśuddhi*). Where [is this stated]? By the passage: "The master, the secret, the wisdom, and then again the fourth likewise"—by this, the meaning of the distinctions between the moments of bliss (*ānanda*) is established.

It is said: by the word *ācārya* (the teacher), the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*)—which is distinct from the joy of friction—is indicated. By the phrase "up to the limit of supreme bliss," the fourth [joy] is indicated; and again, by the word "thus" (*tathā*), the innate joy (*sahajānanda*), characterized by its distinctness, is indicated. In the context of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), there is merely a slight dawning of the innate state. In the context of the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*), there is perfect cognition. But in the context of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), how can there be even the absence of cognition? "It is neither beginning nor end, nor middle; therein there is neither existence nor nirvāṇa. This is that supreme great bliss, neither other nor self. Thus it is said.

Just as sentient beings enter into the state of coemergence (*sahaja*), so too does the Blessed One. This means that the Blessed One also enters into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). By this, it is indicated that the seed-syllable and the moon and sun become blended, which points toward the absence of [conceptual] cognition. By the phrase "having the nature of nectar," the state of coemergence is made firm. [The practitioner] should, in the manner of a mass of rays like the flame of a lamp, gradually bring about non-perception. "Making rays" and "making a mass" refers to the aggregate of the aggregates (*skandha*).

"Gradually" means entering the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in succession, like the flame of a lamp. Just as the flame of a lamp suddenly subsides into the lamp itself, so too do the aggregates of the Blessed One dissolve in sequence: from form (*rūpa*) into form; into feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Form dissolves into feeling, feeling into perception, perception into mental formations, and mental formations into consciousness; then consciousness [dissolves] into space due to the absence of wings. How does the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of Gaurī and the others occur previously? In this regard, the following sequence is taught: having emerged from the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), one unifies the entire triple world and causes it to enter [the aggregates] in due order. Gaurī, having grasped her own objective domain, enters the form of the Blessed One. Likewise, Caurī, Vetālī, and Ghasmarī enter into feeling, perception, and mental formations. Pukkasī, having grasped the solid element (*kaṭhinadhātu*), enters the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) of Vajradhara. Likewise [do] Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī. Water, fire—

They have gone among the Maruts. Although the dissolution of Pukkasī and the others occurs through the dissolutions of Gaurī and the others, and thus a distinction is described, does the dissolution of form and the other [sensory objects] occur by abandoning their own elements, or rather by taking them up simultaneously? Therefore, when there is the grasping of the object, the subject, and the act of grasping even for Pukkasī and the others, through the purification of the three cognitions, they take on the nature of Bhūcarī, Khecarī, and Nairātmyā elsewhere.

The illumination of the world and the non-world is expressed by the term "perception of the world. The goddess Nairātmyā, having occupied both wings within the consciousness of Vajradhara, has gone before all; therefore, one should visualize the syllable *Aṃ* within the moon-maṇḍala at the heart of Nairātmyā. By means of that very syllable *Aṃ* together with the moon-maṇḍala, one should contemplate the Blessed Lady, who has attained a state of innate melting, as having entered the heart of the Blessed Lord. According to this statement, there is the dissolution of the Blessed Lady. By this [process], from the innate [joy] up to the clear light, there is the awakening of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). (22)

Now, the arising from the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) is explained. Now, this clear light is the supreme yoga. Regarding the arising: just as there is the birth of the innate (*sahaja*) from the vajra through the light of gnosis, so too, having begun with the innate and ending with the clear light, one should meditate again from the clear light back to the innate, and from the innate again by this very same sequence, until the attainment of enlightenment occurs. This is according to the sequence of the empowerment of the four junctions—namely, morning, midday, afternoon, and night. Thus ends the section on arising. 23.

The Stages of Meditation (*Bhāvanākrama*): Subsequently, the yogi, weary from meditation, should recite the mantra. Thereafter, having arisen from the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), one should contemplate meditation, mantra-recitation, and the offering (*bali*). Thus, beginning with the Supreme [Heruka] and accomplishing one’s own chosen form through the yoga of Sahaja Hevajra according to the stated sequence, one should then perform the mantra-recitation. Having visualized the Blessed One as consisting of the circle of *ḍākinīs*, one should contemplate the Blessed One first and then the circle of *ḍākinīs*, according to the previous [method], by way of the relationship between cause and effect. Regarding the offering of the *bali*, it is the same; however, in this case, Vajradhara should be visualized in the form of a wrathful deity for the sake of subduing the wicked, relying upon the six-limbed *karmayoga*. Then, regarding the descent of the recitation and the mantra-recitation of Gaurī and the others, whichever [goddess] is being recited, the yoginī should contemplate embracing the Blessed Lady in her abode; this is called the "movement of the yoginī. — Vajradhara.

The recitation (*jāpa*) consists of the root mantra, the eight-syllable mantra, the heart mantra, and the near-heart mantra; or alternatively, the heart mantra of Nairātmyā, Gaurī, and the others should be recited. In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having visualized oneself as the nature of Prajñā in the center of the wheel, by this very method one should rotate the mantra syllables—emerging from the mouth of the deity with rays of light, entering one’s own mouth, being emitted through the path of the *vajra*, and entering the lotus of one’s own deity—and then [emerging] again from the mouth of the deity into one’s own mouth, repeating the mantra in this same sequence without interruption. This is the *dilā-jāpa*.
Having placed the syllables of the mantra upon the sun at the heart, they should be meditated upon as possessing rays and with their heads turned upward. This is the *piṇḍajāpa*.
One should understand that the syllables of those mantras are uttered from the mouths of the Lord of the Mandala and the deities of the Mandala by means of the mind; such is the *samayajāpa*.

Thereafter, one should contemplate [the breath] ascending from the navel. One should contemplate the exhalation (*ucchvāsa*) as it reaches the nose according to one's desire, until the limit of non-perception (*anupalambha*); likewise, one should contemplate the inhalation (*niśvāsa*) below in the same way, according to one's desire, until the limit of non-perception and the realization of soundlessness (*aśabdabodha*). This is the supreme secret oral instruction (*āmnāya*), and thus is the *vajrajāpa*.

Then, having produced the station of Krodheśvara according to the previously stated sequence and having emanated the Krodhas in due order, one should cause them to enter the hosts of obstacles. Having caused the various [deities] to enter with the mantra "Ānaya 2 Oṃ Śumbha Niśumbha," etc., one should contemplate the triad within the City of Liberation according to the three principles (tritattva). ||24||

Having reflected thus, one should generate the *vajra* by means of the withdrawal of the lotus-vessel and likewise the *ghaṇṭā* by means of the earth-vessel. Then, becoming the holder of the *vajra* and *vajraghaṇṭā*, for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, one should perform the empowerment of the *vali*. According to the division of activities and the application of colors, one should summon the Vināyakas who have been brought by those [deities] to the city of Vajradhara—those brought from above by Uṣṇīṣacakravartin and from below by Śumbharāja—having addressed them with the mantra beginning "Oṃ indra yama jala... and so forth. With the words: "Oṃ ākarṣaya jaḥ" (Oṃ, summon! Jaḥ), "Oṃ padmatrayaṃ praveśaya hūṃ" (Oṃ, cause them to enter the three lotuses! Hūṃ), "Oṃ svasvasthāne krodhabandhena bandhaya vaṃ" (Oṃ, bind them in their respective places with the bond of the wrathful ones! Vaṃ), and "Oṃ vajraghaṇṭāyāṃ vaśīkuru hoḥ" (Oṃ, bring them under control in the *vajraghaṇṭā*! Hoḥ)—by this, [one performs] the summoning, entering, binding, and...

Having performed the act of pleasing and produced nectar according to the prescribed method, preceded by worship with flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and so forth, as well as hymns, offerings, and oblations, one should cause the performance of the *sandhyā-gīta* (twilight song) and the *kamalāvarta* and other dances. Thereafter, having formed the *mudrā-bandha* within the embrace, one should visualize the obstructing spirits (*vighnas*). Among the cities of liberation, in the central city, on the eastern petal, is Indra: thousand-eyed, fair-complexioned, holding a thunderbolt in his hand; he is white and seated upon Airāvata. To the south is Yama: holding a staff in his hand, black, and mounted upon a buffalo.

On the western petal is Varuṇa, white, riding upon a makara, with a water-lily and a lotus in his hands. On the northern petal is Yakṣa, yellow, riding upon a man, with a bilva fruit in his hand. All of these wear every ornament and possess jeweled crowns. Yama has the sun as his seat and the radiance of the sun. The remaining deities have the moon as their seats and the radiance of the moon. On the northeastern petal is Bhūtapati (the Lord of Beings), white, three-eyed, wearing a crown of matted hair, riding upon a bull, with the moon as his seat and the radiance of the moon; he holds a trident in his hand, wears a garment of tiger skin, has a body smeared with ashes, is adorned with all ornaments, has the moon as his seat, and possesses the radiance of the moon. In the southeastern petal is Vahni (Fire), pot-bellied, very yellow, dwarfish, riding upon a goat, red in color, holding a rosary and a water-pot, wearing a crown of matted hair, having the sun as his seat and the radiance of the sun, and clad in rags. In the southwestern petal is Rākṣasa.

With disheveled hair, holding a dagger and a skull-cup, wrathful, with a frown, black in color, seated upon a corpse, with the sun as his seat and the radiance of the sun; in the northwest petal is Vāyu, holding a vajra in his hand, dark blue, wearing a jewel crown, having a deer as his vehicle, with the moon as his seat and the radiance of the moon—all [deities] wearing all ornaments. In the central square is Pṛthivī (Earth), yellow, wearing divine garments and all ornaments, holding a jar in her hand, with the moon as her seat and the radiance of the moon; she is joyful, wearing divine garments and all ornaments, holding a jar in her hand, with the moon as her seat and the radiance of the moon.
The pretas stand surrounding the earth; Indra and the other four [directional guardians] all hold dwarf-elephants and nooses, and they all likewise stand in the pratyālīḍha posture.

Upon the eight petals of the lotus situated on the *dharmodayā* above: on the eastern petal is Candra, white, riding a white horse; he wears a jewel crown, holds a water-lily (*kumuda*) in his hand, is adorned with all ornaments, and possesses a moon-seat and moon-like radiance. On the southern petal is Sūrya, red, holding a lotus with both hands, riding a green horse, wearing a jewel crown, adorned with all ornaments, and possessing a sun-seat and sun-like radiance. On the western petal is Budha, yellow, mounted on a mouse, with a sun-seat and sun-like radiance, wearing a jewel crown, and holding an arrow in his hand. On the northern petal is Śukra, blue, with a sun-seat and sun-like radiance, wearing a jewel crown, and holding a spear (*śakti*). On the northeastern petal is Maṅgala, red, with a sun-seat and sun-like radiance, with hair tied upward, and holding a lotus. On the southeastern petal is Bṛhaspati, yellow, with a sun-seat and sun-like radiance, wearing a jewel crown.

Gadādhara says: In the southwestern petal is Śanaiścara (Saturn), who is black with tawny hair, seated upon the sun, possessing the radiance of the sun, and holding a trident. In the northwest petal are Rāhu and Ketu; both are seated upon the sun and possess the radiance of the sun. Rāhu is intensely black, while Ketu is smoke-colored; Rāhu makes the gesture of devouring the wheel of saṃsāra, whereas Ketu holds his hands in the *saṃpuṭa-añjali* (clasped palms) mudrā. In the central pericarp is Brahmā, four-faced and four-armed. He holds a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-pāṇi*). He holds a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in two hands, while with the remaining two arms he supports [the lotus]. He is yellow, has a swan as his vehicle, is seated upon the moon, and possesses the radiance of the moon. He wears a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), is yellow, has matted hair (*jaṭī*), and is short (*kharva*). Surrounding Brahmā are the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Tuṣita, Yāma, and Akaniṣṭha deities, surrounded by other gods. Below, within the *Dharmodaya*, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, are the following: Vāsuki the nāga is yellow; Padma the nāga is white; Karkoṭaka the nāga is red; Takṣaka the nāga is black; Śaṅkhapāla the nāga is yellow; Mahāpadma the nāga is dark green (*śyāma*); Ananta the nāga is pale-white (*pāṇḍara*); and Kulika the nāga is variegated (*karbura*). These eight are adorned with jewel crowns, have human faces, wear all ornaments, and have heads marked by seven hoods. Together with asuras and hell-beings, they surround the pericarp, with Śeṣa at the center.

The white one has a jewel crown, a human face, and is a serpent. Having thus stabilized these [deities] and then transformed them, one should bring them forth in the form of Śrī Heruka through the application of body, speech, and mind. Those standing above should be visualized as having the form of the Body; those in the middle as having the form of Akṣobhya; and those below as having the form of Vāgvajra. For the sake of all ritual activities, their arms and faces should be like those of oneself, and likewise for the [other] deities. For other rites, the syllable *Haṃ* should be employed according to the requirements. Since the form of all is like that of oneself, one should then, with the mantra: *Oṃ pravarasatkārāgra śrīherukārghaṃ pratīccha hūṃ svāhā*, urge them and offer the *argha* (water for the feet) with the conch mudrā. Having offered the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the *saṃdaṃśa* mudrā, one should feed them with the words "Eat this offering! Smell this! and so forth. One should also announce the purpose of the rite. Thereafter, while reciting the twilight song (*sandhyāgīta*) and the mantras of the Lord, the Lady, the goddesses, the assembly, and the wrathful deities, the practitioner holding the vajra and bell should ring the bell with expressive gestures, perform the brandishing of the vajra (*vajrollālana*), and so on. Having recited: *Oṃ akāro mukham...* and so forth, one should say: *Oṃ vajraheruka samayamanupālaya*.

"Abide as Heruka! Be firm for me; be well-pleased with me; be well-nourished by me; be devoted to me; grant me all accomplishments; and in all activities, make my mind auspicious! HŪṂ HA HA HA HA HOḤ! O Blessed Śrī Herukavajra! Do not abandon me, O you who arise from Heruka! Mahāsamayasattva ĀḤ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ! Having satisfied [the deity] with this, one should dismiss him. In this regard, the mantra for dismissal is: OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ PHAṬ (three times). With the syllable OṂ, one makes the aspiration; with the syllable ĀḤ, one satisfies; with the syllable HŪṂ, one brings contentment; with the three PHAṬ syllables, one performs the withdrawal.
The goddesses are the authority, the commitment (samaya) is the authority, and their spoken words are the supreme authority. By this truth, may these goddesses become the cause of my grace.
Those who are unattached to both existence and peace, whose attachment to conceptual constructs has been shattered,
who perceive all phenomena as being like space in their true nature,
and who are oceans of mind with waters of most profound compassion—
O goddesses, show me the utmost compassion! Show it, show it!
By this [process], beginning with the six limbs and ending with the reality of the offering (balitattva), there is the meditative absorption named Karmarājāgrī. ||25||

Having arisen from that, one should visualize a universal vajra-lotus in the center of the *darbha* grass; upon its eight petals, one should visualize the eight [deities] and Īśvara. One should visualize the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in its heart. From the seed-syllable, one should discern the tip of the *nāda*. For the sake of stabilizing the mind, one should contemplate that subtle tip. By becoming one with it, the stabilization of the mind will occur; of this there is no doubt. Through the mere stabilization of the mind, one should emanate the array of Tathāgatas and the vast net of Yoginīs, pervading infinite world-systems. Why? Because the inconceivable Lord, whose nature is the maṇḍala, has emanated from his own sign (*cihna*). The aforementioned sound of the Dharma should be understood as twofold according to the oral instruction. Furthermore, one should contemplate the sign as being merely the size of a mustard seed. This is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "Subtle Yoga. (26)

Having arisen from that, or having performed the two armors through the innate vajra-yoga—beginning with "Akṣobhya in the form of the wheel" and so forth—the yogi should place the wheel upon his head with the syllable *hūṃ*.

*Hrīḥ*: divine earrings on the two ears; *Trāṃ*: a necklace on the throat; *Oṃ*: two bracelets on the hands; *Khaṃ*: a single girdle on the waist; *Haṃ*: one should armor the entire body with the form of ashes, according to the great instruction. Thus, the armor [is performed] for the eyes and so forth with the mantra beginning "Moha-vajrā. In this regard, the armor-mantra is: *Āṃ Āṃ Īṃ Īṃ Ūṃ Ūṃ*. By means of this, the Blessed One’s body is composed of many Vajrayoginīs, Tathāgatas, and so forth. With these two types of armor, the yogi, fully equipped with the great armor, should move about like a lion through the yoga of the coemergent Hevajra. This is the second placement (*nyāsa*). (27)
Wherein? In the midst of the house of the three worlds. And so it is said:
"This peaked pavilion is not the triple world; these living beings are not [ordinary] victors.
I am not a human lord of the wheel, nor are there sense objects, nor sense organs, nor the earth and other elements."

Form and the other [sensory objects] do not exist as having the nature of ultimate reality (dharmatā); these are the deities of the maṇḍala. O mind, as you perceive the entire universe as the maṇḍala-circle, why do you wander in delusion?
Thus ends the section on wandering. ||28||

Thereafter, whatever food or substance has been acquired, or whatever has been obtained by the yogin, all of that—having purified it according to the previously described procedure for tasting nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*) and having empowered it with the three principles (*tritattva*)—is the eating of food. 29.
Then, having explained the procedure for consumption, I shall describe the conduct regarding one's dwelling in accordance with the root mantra. Thus:
one should avoid greed, delusion, fear, anger, shame, and worldly affairs;
casting aside sleep and self-concern, one should practice the conduct—of this there is no doubt.
Having given the gift of the body, one should thereafter undertake the practice;
therefore, no gift is given with a calculation of what is a portion and what is not.
One should consume food and drink exactly as they are obtained;
in this matter, one should not exercise the discrimination of "desirable" or "undesirable."
That which is endowed with five colors is conceived as a single color,
because no distinction is perceived among the many [colors] due to their being a single color.
The auspicious meditation is said to be practiced under a solitary tree, or in a cremation ground,
or likewise at night in a mother’s house, or else in a secluded, remote place.
But when some degree of warmth has been attained, if one wishes to engage in the conduct,
and if there is a desire to attain accomplishment, one should practice by means of this very conduct.

Furthermore, regarding the root [verse], "conduct" (*caryā*) is clearly intended as that which is practiced because it is desired; thus, it is the practice of conduct. It refers to the mode of behavior in one's daily life and worldly dealings, yet from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). What is the meaning of "having attained a higher degree"? What is the meaning of "attaining a slight degree of warmth" (*ūṣmagata*)? One should practice in seclusion in one's own place during the night or at ease until some attainment occurs. Why? Because of the statement: "so that no distinction arises. Once attainment has occurred, whether he establishes a fixed rule or not, he is entirely independent; such is "practice" (*caraṇa*). (30)

Then, at the subsequent twilight, having ceased from activity and directed her mind toward the yoga of the final limit, she should lie down; having visualized the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas at the position of her head, with the intention of prostrating with the eight-limbed bow, she should adopt the lion’s posture for sleep within the yoga of the samādhi of clear light, like the parinirvāṇa of the Blessed One—this is the manner of lying down. ||31||

At the time of rising, one should remain stirred by the songs of the *pukkasi* and other goddesses; having risen, one should act accordingly in this very sequence until the attainment of the maṇḍala-circle. Without that, great enlightenment would not occur. For this very reason, just as the arisen [stage] is not known without the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), so too the generation stage is not known without the yoga of the arisen (*utpannayoga*). And thus it is said in the Tantra: "The teaching of the Dharma for the Vajra-holders relies upon the two stages."

Thus, he is situated within the maṇḍala circle as previously described. He has one face, purified by non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), and two arms, purified by emptiness and compassion (*śūnyatā-karuṇā*). In his right hand is a vajra, which symbolizes indivisible gnosis; in the left, a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*). The *khaṭvāṅga* is the embodiment of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), and the skull-cup symbolizes the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Likewise, he may have four arms and one face, purified by inconceivable gnosis, for the purpose of destroying the four Māras. In his first right arm is a vajra, symbolizing the path of union (*yuganaddha*); in his first left arm is a skull-cup filled with the blood of gods and asuras.

By the word *devāsura* (gods and asuras), there is existence and non-existence. By the word *rakta* (blood), there is their unification. By the word *pūrita* (filled), there is the attainment of that state. This purity is the human skull-cup embraced by Vajravārāhī with her remaining two arms. Thus, he has six arms, which are the purity of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). He has three faces, representing body, speech, and mind. In the left [hands], there is a bell, pure through emptiness (*śūnyatā*). There is a trident for the purpose of cutting through the duality of ignorance; in the right, a vajra, pure through the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*). The flaying knife (*kartikā*) is for cutting through all remaining ignorance. Thus, the two-armed, four-armed, and six-armed forms stand in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) upon a corpse on a sun disk. Furthermore, just as it is in the sixteen-armed form, so it is in these three as well. This is another [mode of] arising. (32)
This *Śrīmatsaroruhapādoddeśasūtra* has been spoken by me according to [his] instruction;
it has been annotated by one known as Jālandhara, relying upon the words of the sages (*ārṣavacana*).
Having composed this *Viśuddhikramatippaṇī* with the vajra of divine play,
may the entire world thereby become the supreme pollen of Vajra-Śrījñāna.

Thus ends the *Vajrapradīpa*, the commentary on the purification of the *Śrīhevajrasādhana* composed by the master Saroruhapāda. This work is the composition of the scholar-master Śrīsūrata. Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; thus speaks the Great Śramaṇa.
It is completed.
